claims.text: Corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection in Q235 steel is influenced by surface passive-layer formation and stability.
A stable passive layer improves the corrosion resistance of Q235 steel.
An unstable passive layer decreases the corrosion resistance of Q235 steel.
The thermodynamic stability of corrosion products governs the corrosion behavior of Q235 steel in aggressive salt.
Impurities in the salt affect the corrosion behavior and passive-layer stability of Q235 steel.
The proposed passive-layer mechanism applies to Q235 steel exposed to aggressive salt at 700–900 °C.
The same proposed mechanism explains protection or degradation across both room-temperature and high-temperature regimes.
Corrosion rate should decrease as temperature increases when a stable passive layer forms.
Changing controlled impurity levels in the salt should change the corrosion rate of Q235 steel.

contradictions.description: The conditions claim coverage of room- and high-temperature regimes, but the intervention and boundary specify only 700–900 °C, so the proposed study does not test the room-temperature regime.
The hypothesis states that the exact temperature dependence is uncertain, while the falsification rule assumes a specific monotonic decrease in corrosion rate with increasing temperature.
